title: Holy laughter
hook: saints often laughed; joy is a fruit of the Spirit
tomorrow: Block close: the shape of a life

segments.voice: Yesterday, in everything give thanks: Paul writing to a grieving church. Your line was in everything, thanks. Which meal did you stop before? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

Three days ago on this path, Abraham was running to feed three strangers at his tent. Today, stay inside with Sarah, listening behind the door. Outside, one of the visitors is saying that Sarah will have a son. Genesis is blunt about it: Abraham and Sarah "were old and well stricken in age." So Sarah does the obvious thing. "Sarah laughed within herself." Quietly. To herself. And the visitor hears it anyway. "Wherefore did Sarah laugh?" She is afraid. "I laughed not." And the answer comes back, almost gently: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." A whole family story in Genesis turns on a laugh. Today, holy laughter.

That first laugh is a hidden one, a laugh of disbelief. Then the promise comes true, and Sarah laughs again, this time out loud and on purpose: "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me." The boy is named Isaac, and readers of the Hebrew hear laughter in the name. The story moves from a laugh behind a door to a laugh the whole neighborhood is invited to share. The Bible keeps a place for that second kind. Ecclesiastes says there is "a time to weep, and a time to laugh." A psalm about coming home from exile says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing." And Jesus, in Luke, makes it a promise: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Paul names joy as part of what grows in a life where God is at work: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace." Joy, right there in the second place, ahead of peace. And Christian memory keeps laughing saints. Tradition says that Lawrence, a deacon of Rome, was put to death on a gridiron and joked with his executioners: turn me over, this side is done. Orthodox Christians honor holy fools, who took Paul's words "we are fools for Christ's sake" at face value. None of this laughs at faith. It's laughter that comes from it. Solemn and holy aren't the same word.
screen: `ALL THAT HEAR WILL LAUGH WITH ME.`
`THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT IS JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let laughter in. Settle, and breathe. Bring back a time you laughed until it hurt. Who was there? What set it off? Replay it slowly: the room, the faces, the moment it tipped over. If a smile comes, let it. If a real laugh comes, let that come too; nobody's grading this. Then think of someone who could use that kind of laugh today. If you pray, you can give thanks for the joy, and for the people you laughed with. The bell holds the time.
Holy laughter. Joy that comes from faith, not at its expense: Sarah's laugh shared with everyone who hears, and joy named among the fruit of the Spirit.
Your line: joy is holy. Today, laugh freely at least once, and share it. Send the funny thing. Tell the story. Let someone laugh with you. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Christians count joy among the fruit of the Spirit; laughter and celebration are part of church life at weddings, baptisms, feasts and fellowship meals, and some traditions tell stories of saints known for their humor.

fork.setup: you're Sarah. you laughed quietly behind the tent door, and the visitor asks why you laughed. what do you say?
options: walk out and argue with him.
fork.reveal: she denies it, because she was afraid. "nay; but thou didst laugh." no punishment follows; later she laughs out loud and invites everyone to laugh with her.

original.note: Hebrew, Genesis 21:6: laughter. "God hath made me to laugh."

trapdoor: what you thought: holy means serious, and laughing in church is out of place.
what it means: joy that comes from faith, from Sarah's shared laugh to joy as a fruit of the Spirit.
what a scholar hears: Genesis plays on laughter across the chapters, and readers of the Hebrew hear it in Isaac's name.

St Lawrence's gridiron joke is a traditional account, introduced with 'tradition says'; confirm the framing and that it is not too grim for this day.
'Orthodox Christians honor holy fools' (e.g. fools-for-Christ saints); confirm fair and that 1 Corinthians 4:10 is the usual scriptural anchor.
Hook superlative (oldest family story) cut in drafting.
'Readers of the Hebrew hear laughter in the name' Isaac: the name and the verb tsachaq; hedged as readers' hearing rather than stated as etymology. Confirm.
Psalm 126 described as 'a psalm about coming home from exile' (v1 'turned again the captivity of Zion'); confirm.
'Joy, right there in the second place' counts from the text of Galatians 5:22.
